documentNotes.title: Full native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface This publication contains 39 theoretical and 14 practical competition problems from the 41st – 45th International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 2009 – 2013. It has been published by the IChO International Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) as a continuation of the preceding Volumes 1 and 2 published on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the IChO with the titles: • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 1, 1st – 20th IChO, 1968 – 1988 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2008). • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 2, 21st – 40th IChO, 1989 – 2008 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2009). Not less than 318 theoretical and 110 practical problems were set in the IChO during the forty-five years of its existence. In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems (numbering the tasks of the particular problems, solution inserted immediately after the text of the problem, solutions without grading points and special graphs used for grading of practical problems). Nevertheless, the mentioned corrections and changes do not concern the contents and language of the competition problems. The practical problems set in the IChO competitions, contain as a rule some instructions, list of apparatuses available, chemicals on each desk and those available in the laboratory, and the risk and safety phrases with regard to the chemicals used. All of these items are important for the competitors during the competition but less important for those who are going to read the competition tasks of this collection and thus, they are omitted. Some parts of the solutions of practical problems are also left out since they require the experimental data which could be obtained by experiments during the practical part of the IChO competition. In this publication SI quantities and units are preferred. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI. Although the numbers of significant figures in the results of some solutions do not obey the criteria generally accepted, they were left without change.

Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and due to the procedure of creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to assign any author's name to a particular problem. Nevertheless, responsibility for the scientific content and language of the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry Olympiads. This review of the competition problems from the 41st – 45th IChO should serve to both competitors and their teachers as a source of further ideas in their preparation for this difficult competition. For those who have taken part in some of these International Chemistry Olympiads the collection of the problems could be of help as archival and documentary material. In the previous forty-five years many known and unknown people - teachers, authors, pupils, and organizers proved their abilities and knowledge and contributed to the success of this already well known and world-wide competition. We wish to all who will organize and attend the future International Chemistry Olympiads, success and happiness. Bratislava, July 2014 Anton Sirota, editor

Source note: This Ankara2011 section prints practical chemical lists, procedures, reference tables/graphs and native evaluation conditions, all retained. Referenced but absent answer sheets, distribution graphs, original points and competitor-dependent results are not invented.

problems.title: Practical problem 1 — Analysis of Chloride Mixtures
problems.statement:
**Introduction**

Composition of a solution containing only MgCl₂ and NaCl can be determined by an indirect titration method, performing precipitation titration to determine total chloride followed by complex-formation titration to determine magnesium ions. A common precipitation technique is the Fajans method. In this argentometric procedure, silver nitrate precipitates chloride; the endpoint is detected by an adsorption indicator, typically dichlorofluorescein, a weak organic acid. Before the endpoint, silver chloride particles are negatively charged by adsorption of excess chloride. Indicator anions are repelled by their negative surface, imparting yellow-green colour. Beyond equivalence, silver chloride particles adsorb silver ions; the positively charged layer attracts dichlorofluoresceinate ions, displaying pink-red colour. Dextrin stabilizes silver chloride particles against coagulation.

Magnesium can be determined by complexometric titration with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). As a hexadentate ligand, EDTA forms chelates with all metal ions except alkali-metal ions in a 1:1 mole ratio regardless of cation charge. Eriochrome Black T (EBT) is common for EDTA titrations. At pH > 7.00, EBT is blue without metal ions and red when coordinated to metal ions. Here chloride in the MgCl₂/NaCl solution is determined by Fajans method and magnesium concentration by EDTA.

A 100 cm³ solution prepared by dissolving MgCl₂ and NaCl in water is the unknown sample. Determine the mass concentration of both salts in g/100 cm³.

**Reagents**

- Unknown solution, 100 cm³.
- Dextrin in three Eppendorf tubes in a zipper bag.
- Dichlorofluorescein indicator.
- AgNO₃ solution, c = 0.1 mol dm⁻³*, 100 cm³.
- EDTA solution, c = 0.01 mol dm⁻³*, 100 cm³.
- pH10 buffer (NH₃/NH₄Cl), 5 cm³.
- Eriochrome Black T indicator.

*The exact concentration is given on the label.

**A. Determination of total chloride concentration by Fajans method**

1. Use a 10 cm³ pipette to transfer a 10.0 cm³ aliquot from “unknown solution” to a 250 cm³ Erlenmeyer flask. Complete to approximately 100 cm³ with distilled water.
2. Take one Eppendorf tube from the zipper bag labelled “dextrin” and transfer all contents to the flask.
3. Add 5 drops of dichlorofluorescein indicator.
4. Record exact AgNO₃ standard-solution concentration.
5. Fill one burette with standard AgNO₃.
6. Titrate until the whole solution is pink-red.
7. Record AgNO₃ volume in cm³.
8. Use the same flask for repeat titration. First pour its contents into “Aqueous Waste” and rinse twice with distilled water.

**B. Determination of Mg²⁺ by direct titration with EDTA**

1. Fill the second burette with standard EDTA.
2. Record its exact concentration.
3. Use a 25 cm³ pipette to transfer a 25.0 cm³ aliquot to a 250 cm³ Erlenmeyer flask. Complete to approximately 100 cm³ with distilled water.
4. Use a 1 cm³ pipette to add 1.0 cm³ pH10 buffer.
5. Add 3–4 drops of EBT.
6. Titrate with standard EDTA until red changes to blue.
7. Record EDTA volume in cm³.
8. Use the same flask for repeats; pour into “Aqueous Waste” and rinse twice with water.

**Treatment of Data**

parts.statement: Determine the amount of Cl⁻ ions in mmol in 100 cm³ of unknown solution.
Determine the amount of Mg²⁺ ions in mmol in 100 cm³ of unknown solution.
Calculate concentrations of both MgCl₂ and NaCl in g/100 cm³ in unknown solution.

solution.statement:
**1.1–1.3**

Some distribution graphs were proposed by the organizer and approved by the International Jury that could be applied for evaluating accuracy of the titrations and consequently awarding points.

For amounts of Cl⁻ and Mg²⁺ and concentrations of MgCl₂ and NaCl in unknown solution, simple stoichiometric calculations can be applied.

problems.title: Practical problem 2 — Hydrogen generation from ammonia borane
problems.statement:
Hydrogen is considered a clean and environmentally benign new energy carrier towards a sustainable future. Effective, safe hydrogen storage is a key issue. Among potent solid chemical-hydride storage materials, ammonia-borane H₃N·BH₃ attracts attention because of high hydrogen content and stability under fuel-cell conditions. Hydrolysis releases hydrogen:

H₃N·BH₃(aq) + 2 H₂O(l) → NH₄BO₂(aq) + 3 H₂(g). (1)

Aqueous ammonia-borane is stable and hydrolysis occurs only with a suitable catalyst. Water-soluble-polymer-stabilized palladium(0) nanoclusters are highly active. They are generated in situ by reducing potassium tetrachloropalladate(II) with ammonia borane in poly(4-styrenesulfonic acid-co-maleic acid).

The experiment starts with potassium tetrachloropalladate(II) precatalyst in polymer solution. Ammonia borane reduces it; polymer-stabilized palladium(0) nanoclusters form and catalyze hydrolysis.

**Chemicals**

- Solution A: H₃NBH₃, 29.5 mg in 10 cm³ H₂O.
- Solution B: poly(4-styrenesulfonic acid-co-maleic acid), 137.7 mg in 9 cm³ H₂O.
- Solution C: potassium tetrachloropalladate(II), K₂[PdCl₄], 6.7 mg in 1 cm³ H₂O.

**I. Preparation of the Experimental Set-up**

1. Check that the setup shown is held on a support, the graduated tube is connected to the Schlenk tube with Tygon tubing and a stir bar is inside the Schlenk tube.
2. Make sure the septum is off and valve open.
3. Change bulb height to adjust the graduated-tube water level to zero.
4. Close the Schlenk-tube valve.

[figure: p2-fig1]

Experimental Set-up.

**II. Hydrolysis of ammonia borane**

**A. In the absence of catalyst**

1. Transfer all Solution A from its glass vial through the funnel to the Schlenk tube.
2. Add Solution B likewise through the funnel.
3. Close with septum, stir at 600 rpm as marked and open the valve to the graduated tube. Record water level V₀ at time zero. Start timer.
4. Every minute read total gas volume and enter the answer-sheet table, for 10 minutes. Stop timer.

**B. In the presence of catalyst**

1. While stirring, inject all Solution C from its glass vial through septum with a 2.0 cm³ syringe. Keep syringe inserted throughout. Start timer.
2. Every minute read total gas volume and enter the answer-sheet table, for 10 minutes. Stop timer.

**Treatment of Data — A. Reaction without catalyst**

parts.statement: Plot recorded gas volume against time in Graph2.1.
Report the gas volume evolved as Vuncatalyzed.
Plot generated gas volume against time in Graph2.2.
Calculate maximum theoretical hydrogen amount in mol and volume in cm³ from hydrolysis of 29.5 mg ammonia borane of purity 97% w/w at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure 690 torr.

Calculate hydrogen-generation rate in your experiment:

(i) In cm³ H₂/min.

(ii) In mmol H₂/min, assuming 25 °C and atmospheric pressure 690 torr.
Based on your experiment calculate hydrogen-production rate per mole of palladium in (mol H₂)(mol Pd)⁻¹(min)⁻¹. Potassium tetrachloropalladate(II) purity is 98% w/w.

problems.title: Practical problem 3 — Synthesis, purification and separation of a diastereomeric mixture
problems.statement:
Nature has many single-enantiomer or diastereomer compounds, such as sugars, amino acids and steroids; some are biologically active drugs. Asymmetric organic synthesis is therefore important. One method employs a metal catalyst coordinated to a chiral organic molecule, a chiral ligand. In this experiment two chiral ligands will be synthesized.

[figure: p3-fig1]

**Chemicals**

- 2,3-dibromo-1-ferrocenylpropan-1-one, 0.50 mmol, labelled “Rxn RB”.
- Triethylamine, 1.0 mmol in 1.0 cm³ CHCl₃, label “V1”.
- (R)-1-phenylethanamine, 1.0 mmol in 0.5 cm³ CHCl₃, label “V2”.
- 2,3-dibromo-1-ferrocenylpropan-1-one, TLC reference starting material, label “SM”.
- Heptane:ethyl acetate mixture, volume ratio 3:2, 500 cm³, label “ELUENT” (source prints “ration”).

**A. Synthesis**

1. Use a syringe to transfer triethylamine in V1 through septum to the 10 cm³ round-bottom reaction flask Rxn RB containing 0.50 mmol 2,3-dibromo-1-ferrocenylpropan-1-one.
2. Stir at room temperature for 30 minutes at 600 rpm as marked.
3. After 30 minutes transfer (R)-1-phenylethanamine in V2 through septum with the same syringe.
4. Stir another 60 minutes at room temperature.
5. Turn off stirrer and perform thin-layer chromatography (TLC):

   i) Check plates; damaged plates are replaced upon request without penalty.

   ii) Draw a pencil start line on the lower portion (Fig3.1).

   iii) Apply SM twice to left spot, then twice to middle. Apply reaction mixture RM once to right and once to middle as Fig3.1; use a different capillary for each sample.

   iv) Develop in TLC chamber with eluent. Mark solvent front with pencil (Fig3.2).

   v) When dry, put plate in zipper bag TLC1.

[figure: p3-fig2]

Figure3.1 TLC plate and Figure3.2 TLC developing chamber.

**B. Flash Column Chromatography**

1. Remove stopper, open valve and bring top-column eluent level to upper silica-gel level (Fig3.3).
2. Close valve and load reaction-flask contents onto flash column with Pasteur pipette.
3. Rinse reaction flask with 0.5 cm³ ELUENT using a clean syringe; load washings with same Pasteur pipette.
4. Open valve and let solvent reach upper silica level.
5. Close valve; add 1.0 cm³ eluent with Pasteur pipette. Open valve; when eluent reaches upper silica level, slowly add 2–3 cm³ without closing valve.
6. Fill column with more eluent. CAUTION: do not disturb silica gel during addition.

[figure: p3-fig3]

Figure3.3 Flash Column Chromatography.

7. Apply little pressure by connecting pressure-applying bulb with an adapter atop the column to accelerate purification. CAUTION: do not apply too much pressure. Add eluent from time to time to prevent silica gel running dry.
8. Collect two major fractions A and B. Discard materials before A and between A and B into “Organic Waste”.
9. Collect first major fraction in a 100 cm³ Erlenmeyer flask and label A.
10. Collect second major fraction in a 250 cm³ Erlenmeyer flask and label B.
11. Close valve after B to stop elution.

**C. Analysis. Perform** (native heading)

1. Perform another TLC: apply SM twice at left, A twice in middle, B five times at right. After development and drying put plate in zipper bag TLC2.
2. Measure A volume with 50 cm³ graduated cylinder; record on answer sheet.
3. Measure B volume with 250 cm³ graduated cylinder; record on answer sheet.
4. Pipette 2.0 cm³ A into 10 cm³ volumetric flask; complete with eluent. Shake, fill UV-visible cell at least ¾ with Pasteur pipette; ask assistant for absorbance at 450 nm and record.
5. Fill another cell at least ¾ with undiluted B using Pasteur pipette; ask assistant for 450 nm absorbance and record.

**Treatment of Data**

parts.statement: Copy (sketch) TLC1 plate on answer sheet.
Copy (sketch) TLC2 plate on answer sheet.
Calculate and record Rf values of A, B and starting material SM spots using TLC2.

Molar extinction coefficient (molar absorptivity) ε is 404 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ for A and 400 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ for B at 450 nm (M = mol dm⁻³). Calculate in percent:

(i) Yield of A based on starting material.

(ii) Yield of B based on starting material.

solution.statement:
**3.1–3.2** Maximum points are given:

- For three spots loaded on the baseline.
- For well-developed, separated TLC spots.
- For solvent-front line and baseline.
- For accurate presentation of the TLC sketch.
- In3.2 additionally for absence of B in A and vice versa.

**3.3** Maximum points when calculated and recorded Rf values fall within:

| Spots | Rf |
|---|---|
| Fraction A | 0.40–0.50 |
| Fraction B | 0.20–0.30 |
| Starting material SM | 0.65–0.75 |

**3.4** Points were awarded according to distribution graphs proposed by the organizer and approved by the International Jury, applied to A and B when evaluating volumes, absorbance and yields.
